plain_summary: The Commisso Lab studies pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), one of the deadliest cancers, focusing on how tumor cells and their surrounding support tissue adapt to survive harsh, nutrient-poor conditions. A major theme is macropinocytosis, a form of "cellular drinking" that cancer cells use to scavenge external proteins for nutrients like amino acids when normal supplies such as glutamine run short. The lab also studies cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which shape the tumor's surrounding stroma and immune environment, and how factors like aging and metabolic stress change CAF behavior in ways that suppress the immune system. Other work identifies specific molecules, such as PI5P4Kα, MICAL2, and PSGL-1, that tumors depend on and that could be drugged. Together, this research aims to find new therapeutic targets and combination strategies that make pancreatic cancer more vulnerable to existing treatments like immunotherapy and chemotherapy.
trajectory: Recent work (2025-2026) is moving from mechanistic studies of macropinocytosis and CAF metabolism toward translational, combination-therapy questions: how metabolic and stromal interventions (blocking macropinocytosis, targeting PI5P4Kα, disabling PSGL-1) can sensitize PDAC to immunotherapy and chemotherapy. A newer thread examines how the aging tumor microenvironment specifically drives immune exclusion and metastasis, pointing toward age-stratified, stroma-targeted therapeutic strategies alongside continued mechanistic work on nutrient scavenging and organellar pH as druggable vulnerabilities.
